parts.partTitle: Part 8: Cron, Systemd, and Scheduled Automation

blocks.value: Cron: The Classic Task Scheduler

Cron is Linux's time-based job scheduler. It runs commands at specified intervals — every minute, every hour, every day at 2 AM, every Monday, etc. The crontab (cron table) is a per-user configuration file that defines when and what to run. Cron syntax has five fields: minute (0-59), hour (0-23), day of month (1-31), month (1-12), day of week (0-7, where both 0 and 7 are Sunday). Special characters include * (any value), , (list), - (range), and / (step). Cron is perfect for backups, log rotation, report generation, and periodic maintenance.

# CRON SYNTAX
# .---------------- minute (0 - 59)
# |  .------------- hour (0 - 23)
# |  |  .---------- day of month (1 - 31)
# |  |  |  .------- month (1 - 12)
# |  |  |  |  .---- day of week (0 - 7, 0 and 7 = Sunday)
# |  |  |  |  |
# *  *  *  *  *  command to execute

# MANAGE CRONTAB

# Edit your crontab
crontab -e

# List your crontab entries
crontab -l

# Remove all crontab entries
crontab -r

# COMMON SCHEDULES

# Every minute
* * * * * /path/to/script.sh

# Every 5 minutes
*/5 * * * * /path/to/script.sh

# Every hour at minute 0
0 * * * * /path/to/script.sh

# Every 2 hours
0 */2 * * * /path/to/script.sh

# Daily at 2:30 AM
30 2 * * * /path/to/script.sh

# Daily at 2:30 AM on weekdays only
30 2 * * 1-5 /path/to/script.sh

# Weekly on Sunday at 3 AM
0 3 * * 0 /path/to/script.sh

# Monthly on the 1st at 4 AM
0 4 1 * * /path/to/script.sh

# Every 15 minutes during business hours (9-5)
*/15 9-17 * * 1-5 /path/to/script.sh

# Twice daily at 8 AM and 6 PM
0 8,18 * * * /path/to/script.sh

# CRON ENVIRONMENT

# Set environment variables in crontab
SHELL=/bin/bash
PATH=/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin
MAILTO=admin@example.com
HOME=/home/user

# Run with specific environment
* * * * * cd /app && /usr/bin/python3 script.py

# REDIRECT OUTPUT

# Log output to file
* * * * * /path/to/script.sh >> /var/log/script.log 2>&1

# Discard output
* * * * * /path/to/script.sh > /dev/null 2>&1

# Log stdout and stderr separately
* * * * * /path/to/script.sh >> /var/log/script.out.log 2>> /var/log/script.err.log

# SPECIAL DIRECTORIES (no crontab needed)
# Place scripts in these directories (must be executable):
# /etc/cron.hourly/    — Run every hour
# /etc/cron.daily/     — Run every day
# /etc/cron.weekly/    — Run every week
# /etc/cron.monthly/   — Run every month

# TIMING TIP: Spread out cron jobs
# Bad:  0 0 * * *  (midnight — everyone does this)
# Good: 17 3 * * *  (3:17 AM — spreads server load)

blocks.value: Systemd Timers: Modern Cron Replacement

Systemd timers are the modern replacement for cron on most Linux distributions. They offer advantages: dependency management (services can depend on network being up), logging through journalctl, easier debugging, and more flexible timing (including calendar events and monotonic timers). A systemd timer consists of two files: a .service file defining what to run, and a .timer file defining when to run it. Timers can be real-time (calendar-based, like cron) or monotonic (relative to boot or previous run).

# SYSTEMD TIMER EXAMPLE

# 1. Create the service file
# /etc/systemd/system/backup.service

[Unit]
Description=Daily Backup Service
After=network.target

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/backup.sh
User=backup
Group=backup
StandardOutput=journal
StandardError=journal

# 2. Create the timer file
# /etc/systemd/system/backup.timer

[Unit]
Description=Run backup daily at 2 AM

[Timer]
OnCalendar=*-*-* 02:00:00
Persistent=true
# If system was off at 2 AM, run when it comes back

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target

# 3. Enable and start the timer
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable backup.timer
sudo systemctl start backup.timer

# MANAGE TIMERS

# List all timers
systemctl list-timers

# List timers (including inactive)
systemctl list-timers --all

# Check timer status
systemctl status backup.timer

# Check service status
systemctl status backup.service

# View timer logs
journalctl -u backup.service
journalctl -u backup.timer

# TIMER TYPES

# Real-time (calendar-based)
[Timer]
OnCalendar=Mon-Fri *-*-* 09:00:00    # Weekdays at 9 AM
OnCalendar=*-*-01 03:00:00           # 1st of every month at 3 AM
OnCalendar=weekly                    # Alias for Mon 00:00:00
OnCalendar=daily                     # Alias for 00:00:00
OnCalendar=hourly                    # Alias for :00:00

# Monotonic (relative timers)
[Timer]
OnBootSec=5min           # 5 minutes after boot
OnUnitActiveSec=1h       # 1 hour after last activation
OnUnitInactiveSec=30min  # 30 minutes after last deactivation

# Combined
[Timer]
OnBootSec=10min
OnUnitActiveSec=1h

# ACCURACY AND RANDOMIZATION

[Timer]
AccuracySec=1h           # Timer accuracy (saves power)
RandomizedDelaySec=600   # Random delay up to 10 minutes
# Prevents thundering herd when many timers trigger simultaneously

# USER-SPECIFIC TIMERS (no root needed)
# ~/.config/systemd/user/my-timer.timer
# ~/.config/systemd/user/my-timer.service

systemctl --user daemon-reload
systemctl --user enable my-timer.timer
systemctl --user start my-timer.timer
systemctl --user list-timers

blocks.value: At and Batch: One-Time Scheduling

While cron and systemd timers handle recurring tasks, at schedules one-time future execution. Want to run a command at 11 PM tonight? Use at. The batch command is similar but runs when system load is low. These are simpler than cron for ad-hoc scheduling — no need to edit a crontab and remember to remove the entry later. atq lists pending jobs; atrm removes them.

# AT: One-time scheduling

# Install at if not present
sudo apt-get install at

# Schedule a command for later
at 11:00 PM today
# Type commands, then Ctrl+D to save
# > /usr/local/bin/backup.sh
# > echo "Backup done" | mail -s "Backup" admin@example.com
# > [Ctrl+D]

# Schedule with explicit time
at 14:30 tomorrow
at now + 2 hours
at now + 30 minutes
at  midnight
at teatime           # 4 PM
at today
at tomorrow
at noon
at 2024-12-25 09:00

# Schedule from file
at 2:00 AM tomorrow -f /path/to/script.sh

# List pending jobs
atq
# Output: 1   Thu Aug 1 23:00:00 2026 a alice

# Remove a pending job
atrm 1

# View job details
at -c 1

# BATCH: Run when system load permits

# Run command when load average drops below 1.5
batch
# > /usr/local/bin/heavy-processing.sh
# > [Ctrl+D]

# Check batch queue
atq

# Both at and batch use the same queue system
# at runs at specific time; batch runs when load permits

blocks.value: Anacron: For Systems That Are Not Always On

Anacron is designed for desktops and laptops that are not running 24/7. Unlike cron, which skips missed jobs if the system is off, anacron runs missed jobs when the system comes back. It is perfect for daily backups on a laptop — if you shut down at night, the backup runs when you boot in the morning. Anacron only supports daily, weekly, and monthly frequencies, not the fine-grained timing of cron. Most modern systems run both cron and anacron together.

# ANACRON CONFIGURATION
# /etc/anacrontab

# Format: period delay job-identifier command
# period   = days between runs (1=daily, 7=weekly, 30=monthly)
# delay    = minutes to wait after boot before running
# job-id   = unique name for the job (used for timestamp file)
# command  = the command to run

# Example /etc/anacrontab:
SHELL=/bin/sh
PATH=/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/sbin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin

# period  delay  job-id          command
1         5      daily-backup    /usr/local/bin/backup.sh
7         10     weekly-cleanup  /usr/local/bin/cleanup.sh
30        15     monthly-report  /usr/local/bin/generate-report.sh

# Anacron stores timestamps in /var/spool/anacron/
# daily-backup → /var/spool/anacron/daily-backup

# Check when jobs last ran
ls -la /var/spool/anacron/

# Force run a job immediately
sudo anacron -f -n daily-backup
# -f = force, -n = now

# Anacron logs
sudo tail /var/log/syslog | grep anacron

# USER ANACRON (modern alternative)
# Use systemd user timers with Persistent=true
# This achieves the same result as anacron

# COMBINING CRON AND ANACRON
# Most systems have /etc/cron.daily, /etc/cron.weekly, /etc/cron.monthly
# These are run by anacron (if installed) or by run-parts from cron
# Anacron takes precedence when both are installed

# Check which scheduler runs these directories
ls -la /etc/cron.d/
# Look for anacron entry that runs run-parts on the directories

blocks.question: What is the main advantage of systemd timers over traditional cron?
options: They are older and more widely supported
They integrate with system dependencies, provide better logging via journalctl, and support more flexible timing
They require less configuration
They can only run as root
blocks.correctAnswer: They integrate with system dependencies, provide better logging via journalctl, and support more flexible timing
blocks.explanation: Systemd timers offer dependency management (wait for network, etc.), unified logging through journalctl, calendar events beyond cron's syntax, monotonic timers (relative to boot), and better debugging with systemctl status. They are the modern standard on most Linux distributions, though cron remains widely used for simplicity.

blocks.value: Tmux and Screen: Terminal Multiplexers

Terminal multiplexers let you run multiple terminal sessions inside one window, detach and reattach sessions, and persist work across disconnections. This is essential for remote work — start a long-running process on a server, disconnect your laptop, and reconnect hours later to find the process still running. Tmux is the modern standard; Screen is the older alternative. Tmux features windows (tabs), panes (splits), sessions (workspaces), and extensive customization.

# TMUX BASICS

# Start a new session
tmux
# or with name:
tmux new -s myproject

# Detach from session (keep it running)
# Press Ctrl+B, then D

# List sessions
tmux ls

# Attach to existing session
tmux attach -t myproject
# or shorthand:
tmux a -t myproject

# Attach to last session
tmux attach

# Kill a session
tmux kill-session -t myproject

# WINDOWS (like tabs)
# Ctrl+B, C     = Create new window
# Ctrl+B, N     = Next window
# Ctrl+B, P     = Previous window
# Ctrl+B, 0-9   = Switch to window number
# Ctrl+B, W     = List windows (interactive)
# Ctrl+B, ,     = Rename current window
# Ctrl+B, &     = Kill current window

# PANES (splits)
# Ctrl+B, %     = Split vertically
# Ctrl+B, "     = Split horizontally
# Ctrl+B, arrow = Move between panes
# Ctrl+B, O     = Cycle through panes
# Ctrl+B, X     = Kill current pane
# Ctrl+B, Z     = Zoom current pane (toggle)
# Ctrl+B, space = Cycle through pane layouts

# SESSION MANAGEMENT
# Ctrl+B, D     = Detach
# Ctrl+B, S     = List all sessions (interactive)
# Ctrl+B, $     = Rename session
# Ctrl+B, (     = Previous session
# Ctrl+B, )     = Next session

# CONFIGURATION (~/.tmux.conf)
# Better prefix key (Caps Lock as Ctrl is recommended)
# unbind C-b
# set -g prefix C-a
# bind C-a send-prefix

# Mouse support
# set -g mouse on

# Start window numbering at 1
# set -g base-index 1

# Vim-style pane navigation
# bind h select-pane -L
# bind j select-pane -D
# bind k select-pane -U
# bind l select-pane -R

# SCREEN (legacy, but still found on older systems)

# Start new session
screen -S mysession

# Detach: Ctrl+A, D
# List: screen -ls
# Attach: screen -r mysession
# Kill: screen -S mysession -X quit

blocks.value: Vim: The Editor You Cannot Avoid

Vim is a modal text editor — it has different modes for navigating, inserting text, and executing commands. The learning curve is steep, but the productivity payoff is enormous. Vim is installed on virtually every Unix system, making it the only editor guaranteed to be available when you SSH into a server. Understanding basic Vim (open, edit, save, quit) is essential; mastering Vim transforms your editing speed. Start with vimtutor (run it in your terminal) for a 30-minute interactive tutorial.

# VIM MODES

# Insert  = Typing text (press i to enter from Normal)
# Visual  = Selecting text (press v to enter)

vim                   # Open empty buffer

blocks.value: Modern CLI Tools Ecosystem

The modern command line has evolved beyond traditional Unix tools. New tools replace or enhance classics with better defaults, colors, and usability. fzf provides fuzzy finding for files, history, and any list. ripgrep (rg) replaces grep with faster, smarter searching. fd replaces find with simpler syntax. bat replaces cat with syntax highlighting. exa replaces ls with icons and git integration. These tools make the terminal more productive and pleasant without sacrificing power.

# MODERN CLI TOOLS

# FZF: Fuzzy finder
# Install: git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/junegunn/fzf.git ~/.fzf && ~/.fzf/install

# Interactive file finder
fzf

# Find file and open in vim
vim $(fzf)

# Search command history
# Press Ctrl+R (after fzf key bindings setup)

# Search in specific directory
ls /var/log | fzf

# Use in scripts
selected=$(find . -type f | fzf)
echo "You selected: $selected"

# RIPGREP (rg): Fast grep replacement
# Install: sudo apt-get install ripgrep (or cargo install ripgrep)

# Search in current directory
rg "pattern"

# Search specific file type
rg "function" --type js

# Search and show context
rg "pattern" -C 3

# Search in hidden files too
rg "pattern" --hidden

# Respect .gitignore by default (unlike grep)
# Use --no-ignore to search ignored files

# FD: User-friendly find
# Install: sudo apt-get install fd-find (may be fdfind)

# Find files by name
fd "*.txt"

# Find and execute command
fd "*.log" -x rm

# Find in specific directory
fd "*.py" src/

# Find including hidden files
fd "*.conf" --hidden

# BAT: Syntax-highlighting cat replacement
# Install: sudo apt-get install bat (may be batcat)

# View file with syntax highlighting
bat file.py

# Show line numbers
bat --style=numbers file.py

# Show git modifications
bat --diff file.py

# EXA: Enhanced ls
# Install: sudo apt-get install exa

# List with icons and git status
exa --icons --git

# Tree view
exa --tree

# Show file sizes
exa -lh

# LAZYGIT: Terminal UI for Git
# Install: go install github.com/jesseduffield/lazygit@latest

# Launch TUI
lazygit

# Navigate with arrow keys, press ? for help

# HTOP: Interactive process viewer (mentioned earlier)
# Install: sudo apt-get install htop

# BTOP: Even prettier system monitor
# Install: sudo snap install btop

# JQ: JSON processor (covered in scripting section)
# Install: sudo apt-get install jq

# YQ: YAML processor (like jq for YAML)
# Install: pip install yq

# ALIASES FOR MODERN TOOLS
# Add to ~/.bashrc:
# alias cat='bat --paging=never'
# alias ls='exa --icons'
# alias ll='exa -lah --icons --git'
# alias find='fd'
# alias grep='rg'
# alias top='htop'

blocks.value: Package Managers and Software Installation

Linux distributions use different package managers: apt (Debian/Ubuntu), dnf/yum (Fedora/RHEL/CentOS), pacman (Arch), zypper (openSUSE). Beyond system packages, language-specific managers (pip, npm, gem, cargo) install libraries and tools. Universal package managers like Snap, Flatpak, and AppImage distribute applications across distributions. For developers, understanding when to use each manager prevents dependency conflicts and broken systems. The golden rule: use the system package manager for system tools, language managers for development libraries, and universal managers for desktop applications.

# APT (Debian, Ubuntu, Mint)

# Update package lists
sudo apt-get update

# Upgrade installed packages
sudo apt-get upgrade
# or full upgrade (handles dependencies better):
sudo apt-get full-upgrade

# Install package
sudo apt-get install nginx

# Remove package
sudo apt-get remove nginx
# or remove with configuration:
sudo apt-get purge nginx

# Search for package
apt-cache search nginx

# Show package info
apt-cache show nginx

# Clean up
sudo apt-get autoremove     # Remove unused dependencies
sudo apt-get clean          # Clear downloaded package files

# DNF (Fedora, RHEL, CentOS)

sudo dnf update
sudo dnf install nginx
sudo dnf remove nginx
sudo dnf search nginx
sudo dnf info nginx

# PACMAN (Arch, Manjaro)

sudo pacman -Sy           # Update package lists
sudo pacman -S nginx      # Install
sudo pacman -R nginx      # Remove
sudo pacman -Ss nginx     # Search
sudo pacman -Syu          # Update system

# LANGUAGE-SPECIFIC MANAGERS

# Python: pip
pip install requests
pip install --user requests    # Install for current user only
pip uninstall requests
pip list
pip freeze > requirements.txt  # Export dependencies
pip install -r requirements.txt # Install from file

# Node.js: npm
npm install -g typescript      # Global install
npm install lodash             # Local install (in project)
npm uninstall lodash
npm list
npm update

# Rust: cargo
cargo install ripgrep
cargo uninstall ripgrep

# UNIVERSAL PACKAGE MANAGERS

# Snap (Ubuntu, works on most distros)
sudo snap install code --classic    # VS Code
sudo snap install spotify
sudo snap remove spotify
sudo snap list

# Flatpak (works everywhere)
flatpak install flathub com.spotify.Client
flatpak uninstall com.spotify.Client
flatpak list

# Homebrew (macOS and Linux)
brew install wget
brew uninstall wget
brew list
brew update && brew upgrade

This final exam tests your understanding across all parts of the course. Try to answer each question before checking the explanation. A score of 80% or higher means you are ready to use the command line confidently in real work.

blocks.question: What is the difference between `rm -r folder/` and `rm -rf folder/`?
options: They do exactly the same thing
`-rf` forces removal without confirmation; `-r` may prompt for write-protected files
`-r` removes files; `-rf` removes only empty directories
`-rf` creates a backup first; `-r` does not
blocks.correctAnswer: `-rf` forces removal without confirmation; `-r` may prompt for write-protected files
blocks.explanation: Both `rm -r` and `rm -rf` recursively remove directories. The `-f` (force) flag suppresses most error messages and ignores non-existent files, and prevents prompts for write-protected files. Without `-f`, `rm -r` will ask for confirmation before removing write-protected files. The `-rf` combination is extremely dangerous — it will delete anything without asking.

blocks.question: You need to find all `.log` files larger than 50MB modified more than 7 days ago and delete them. Which command is correct?
options: find . -name '*.log' -size +50M -mtime +7 -delete
find . -name '*.log' -size 50M -mtime 7 -rm
grep -r '*.log' | awk '$5 > 50M' | xargs rm
ls -la | grep '.log' | grep '50M' | rm
blocks.explanation: `find . -name '*.log'` finds all .log files in current directory and subdirectories. `-size +50M` filters for files larger than 50MB. `-mtime +7` filters for files modified more than 7 days ago. `-delete` removes the matched files. The other options either use wrong syntax (`-rm` is not a find action), wrong tools (grep cannot filter by file size), or wrong approach (piping filenames to rm without xargs).

blocks.question: What does the pipeline `cat access.log | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -10` produce?
options: The 10 most recent log entries
The top 10 IP addresses by number of requests, sorted from most to least frequent
The first 10 lines of the log file
A list of 10 unique URLs accessed
blocks.correctAnswer: The top 10 IP addresses by number of requests, sorted from most to least frequent
blocks.explanation: This is a classic log analysis pipeline: `cat access.log` outputs the log file. `awk '{print $1}'` extracts the first column (IP address in Apache/Nginx combined log format). `sort` groups identical IPs together. `uniq -c` counts occurrences of each IP. `sort -nr` sorts numerically in reverse order (highest count first). `head -10` shows only the top 10. The result is the 10 most active IP addresses.

blocks.question: In a shell script, why should you write `"$var"` instead of `$var`?
options: It makes the variable name easier to read
It prevents word splitting and globbing on the variable's value
It makes the script run faster
It is required for all variable names longer than 3 characters
blocks.correctAnswer: It prevents word splitting and globbing on the variable's value
blocks.explanation: Without quotes, Bash performs word splitting on the variable's value — if `$var` contains 'hello world', it becomes two separate arguments. It also performs globbing (filename expansion) on special characters like `*` and `?`. Quoting `"$var"` preserves the value as a single argument and prevents unexpected expansion. This is one of the most common bugs in shell scripts. Always quote your variables unless you specifically want word splitting.

blocks.question: You run a script with `set -euo pipefail` at the top. The script contains `grep 'pattern' file.txt | wc -l`. If `grep` fails because the file does not exist, what happens?
options: The script continues because `wc -l` succeeds
The script exits immediately because `pipefail` causes the entire pipeline to fail
The script prints an error but continues
The script ignores the error because `grep` errors are not critical
blocks.correctAnswer: The script exits immediately because `pipefail` causes the entire pipeline to fail
blocks.explanation: `set -e` makes the script exit on any command failure. `set -o pipefail` extends this to pipelines — if any command in a pipe fails, the entire pipeline's exit status reflects that failure, triggering `set -e`. Without `pipefail`, the pipeline's exit status would be that of the last command (`wc -l`), which would succeed even if `grep` failed, masking the error. This combination is essential for catching errors in pipelines.

blocks.question: You need to schedule a script to run every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday at 3:15 AM. What is the correct cron expression?
blocks.explanation: Cron fields are: minute, hour, day-of-month, month, day-of-week. 3:15 AM means minute=15, hour=3. Monday=1, Wednesday=3, Friday=5 in the day-of-week field. The `,` operator lists multiple values. So `15 3 * * 1,3,5` means: at minute 15, hour 3, any day of month, any month, on days 1, 3, and 5 of the week. Option B reverses minute and hour. Option C puts days in the wrong field. Option D runs every weekday, not Mon/Wed/Fri.

blocks.question: What is the purpose of the `trap` command in shell scripts?
options: To catch syntax errors before the script runs
To execute cleanup code when the script receives signals or exits
To debug the script by printing variable values
To prevent the script from being run by unauthorized users
blocks.correctAnswer: To execute cleanup code when the script receives signals or exits
blocks.explanation: `trap` catches signals (like SIGINT from Ctrl+C, SIGTERM from kill) and the EXIT pseudo-signal. It ensures cleanup code runs regardless of how the script terminates — success, error, or interruption. For example, `trap cleanup EXIT` runs the `cleanup` function when the script exits for any reason. This is essential for removing temporary files, releasing locks, and closing connections.

blocks.question: You are working on a remote server via SSH and start a long-running database migration. Your internet connection is unstable. What is the best way to ensure the migration continues even if your connection drops?
options: Run it normally and hope the connection stays stable
Use `nohup ./migrate.sh &` before starting the command
Start a `tmux` session, run the command inside it, then detach
Use `kill -9` on the SSH process to force it to stay open
blocks.correctAnswer: Start a `tmux` session, run the command inside it, then detach
blocks.explanation: `tmux` creates a persistent terminal session on the server. You start the migration inside tmux, detach with Ctrl+B then D, and the session (and your command) keeps running on the server even if your SSH connection drops. Later, you SSH back in and reattach with `tmux attach`. `nohup` also works but does not give you the ability to reattach and view progress. `kill -9` on SSH would actually terminate the connection and your process.

blocks.question: You have a script that should create a backup, but you want it to use a default backup directory if the user does not provide one as an argument. Which syntax accomplishes this?
options: BACKUP_DIR=$1
BACKUP_DIR=${1:-/backup/default}
BACKUP_DIR=$1 || /backup/default
BACKUP_DIR=default($1, /backup/default)
blocks.explanation: `${1:-/backup/default}` is parameter expansion with a default value. If `$1` is unset or empty, it evaluates to `/backup/default`. If `$1` is set, it uses the provided value. Option A would set BACKUP_DIR to empty if no argument is given. Option C uses `||` which tests exit status, not emptiness. Option D is not valid Bash syntax. This pattern is extremely common for scripts with optional arguments.

blocks.question: A file has permissions `-rwxr-xr--`. What can the group members do with this file?
options: Read, write, and execute it
Read and execute it, but not modify it
Only read it
Nothing at all
blocks.correctAnswer: Read and execute it, but not modify it
blocks.explanation: The permission string `-rwxr-xr--` breaks down as: `-` = regular file, `rwx` = owner has read, write, execute, `r-x` = group has read and execute but NOT write, `r--` = others have only read. So group members (the middle `r-x` triplet) can read the file and execute it if it is a program/script, but they cannot modify it because the `w` permission is missing. This is a common permission pattern for shared executables.

blocks.question: Which command correctly creates a compressed archive named `project-backup.tar.gz` containing the `src/`, `config/`, and `docs/` directories while excluding all `.git` directories and `.tmp` files?
options: tar -czvf project-backup.tar.gz src/ config/ docs/ --exclude='.git' --exclude='*.tmp'
zip -r project-backup.tar.gz src/ config/ docs/ -x .git -x *.tmp
tar -czvf project-backup.tar.gz --exclude='.git' --exclude='*.tmp' src/ config/ docs/
gzip -r project-backup.tar.gz src/ config/ docs/
blocks.explanation: The `--exclude` patterns must come BEFORE the directory arguments in tar. `tar -czvf` creates a gzip-compressed archive (`-c` create, `-z` gzip, `-v` verbose, `-f` file). The exclude patterns filter out `.git` directories and `.tmp` files. Option A places excludes after directories, which may not work in all tar versions. Option B uses zip with wrong extension. Option D uses `gzip -r` which compresses individual files, not creating an archive.
